name: Apache Pulsar
summary: A multi-tenant messaging and streaming platform from Yahoo that keeps brokers stateless and stores messages in Apache BookKeeper, so one topic can serve as a log, a pub-sub feed or a work queue.
intro: Pulsar splits serving from storage. Brokers are stateless: each topic is owned by one broker, which takes writes from producers, dispatches messages to consumers and serves most reads from a cache. The messages themselves live in Apache BookKeeper, a separate cluster of storage nodes called bookies. A topic is stored as a managed ledger made of many BookKeeper ledgers, append-only logs with a single writer whose entries are copied to several bookies; consumer positions (cursors) are stored there too. Because brokers hold no data, a topic can move to another broker in seconds, and storage grows by adding bookies. A metadata store keeps cluster state: Oxia (recommended for new clusters) or Apache ZooKeeper, and RocksDB in standalone mode. Old data can be offloaded with tiered storage to Amazon S3, Google Cloud Storage, Azure Blob Storage or a file system, and clients still read it as if nothing changed.

Topics are named `persistent://tenant/namespace/topic`. Tenants and namespaces are built in, with their own authentication, quotas, retention and isolation policies, so one cluster can serve many teams. How a topic behaves depends on the subscription: exclusive (one consumer, the default), failover (one active consumer with standbys), shared (round-robin across consumers, each message acknowledged individually, no ordering) and key_shared (spread across consumers but each key always goes to the same one). A unique subscription per consumer gives pub-sub fan-out; a shared subscription turns the same topic into a queue, with delayed delivery, negative acks, retry and dead-letter topics. Geo-replication copies topic data between clusters in different regions. Pulsar Functions run small Java, Python or Go functions on each message inside the cluster, and Pulsar IO connectors move data to and from systems such as Kafka and Cassandra. Pulsar 5.0 (October 2026), the newest long-term-support release, adds scalable topics that split and merge key ranges as load changes, instead of a fixed partition count.
strengths: Brokers and storage scale separately: stateless brokers take over topics in seconds, and adding bookies adds storage capacity right away
One system for streaming and queuing, chosen per subscription (exclusive, failover, shared, key_shared), with delayed delivery and dead-letter topics built in
Multi-tenancy and geo-replication are part of the core, from Yahoo’s need to run messaging as a hosted service across 10+ data centres
Tiered storage offloads old backlog to S3, GCS or Azure Blob, so long retention doesn’t need large bookie disks
limits: More to run than a single-binary broker: brokers, a BookKeeper cluster and a metadata store, plus a configuration store for multi-cluster setups
Each topic is served by one broker, so a hot topic needs partitions (or 5.0’s scalable topics) to spread load
Shared subscriptions give up ordering, and key_shared needs producers to disable batching or batch by key
No Kafka protocol in the core, and the Kafka-on-Pulsar protocol handler is archived (last updated January 2024), so moving data between Kafka and Pulsar goes through Pulsar IO connectors

story: Yahoo needed one messaging service for many of its products, run centrally with applications onboarded as tenants. It wanted publish latencies around 5 ms on average and under 15 ms at the 99th percentile, durability with every message on several disks, replication between data centres, and support for a million topics. Finding no open-source system that met all of that, its team built Pulsar and deployed the first instance in the second quarter of 2015.

Pulsar was built on Apache BookKeeper, a distributed write-ahead log that Yahoo had open-sourced in 2011, with ZooKeeper for coordination. By September 2016, when Yahoo open-sourced Pulsar under Apache 2.0, it ran in more than 10 data centres with full-mesh replication and over 1.4 million topics, behind Yahoo Mail, Finance, Sports and Gemini Ads. The project entered the Apache Incubator on 1 June 2017 and graduated to a top-level project in September 2018, by which time it had added Pulsar Functions and the Pulsar IO connector framework.
The project now numbers releases as LTS.feature.patch: 4.0 (October 2024) and 5.0 (October 2026) are long-term-support lines, and 5.0 has active support until October 2028.

choices.choice: Separate stateless brokers from BookKeeper storage
choices.why: Brokers that hold no data can hand topics to each other within seconds, and BookKeeper’s separate journal and storage disks keep consumers draining a backlog from slowing down publishers. The ASF called this two-layer design a key strength at graduation.
Yahoo ran Pulsar as a hosted service for many teams, so tenants, namespaces, quotas and access control are core concepts rather than conventions.

choices.choice: Subscription modes instead of separate products
choices.why: An exclusive subscription behaves like a JMS topic and a shared one like a JMS queue, so the same stored topic serves both patterns.

choices.choice: Replication between data centres in the core
choices.why: Yahoo had users in many regions who created global topics; brokers asynchronously push messages published locally to remote clusters.
